title: Internal Medicine Overview
subject: Medicine
summary: Internal medicine integrates clinical reasoning across organ systems, focusing on common tropical diseases, limited diagnostics, and bedside management. It trains students to prioritize investigations, recognise red flags, and apply evidence‑based treatment in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Internal medicine is the specialty that manages adult patients with undifferentiated medical problems, using history, physical exam and targeted investigations to reach a working diagnosis.
b: Diagnose by pattern recognition: symptom clusters, organ‑specific signs, and epidemiologic context.
Use WHO/UNICEF case definitions for TB, malaria, HIV when definitive tests are unavailable.

sections.p: Severity is graded by organ‑specific scores (e.g., CURB‑65 for pneumonia, Child‑Pugh for cirrhosis) and by systemic markers such as shock, altered mental status, or multi‑organ failure.
b: Identify high‑risk patients early to trigger escalation.

sections.p: Consider common tropical and low‑resource aetiologies before rare ones. Categorise by infection, non‑communicable disease, and environmental exposures.
b: Infections: malaria, TB, HIV‑related opportunists, bacterial sepsis.
Non‑communicable: hypertension, diabetes, sickle‑cell disease, rheumatic heart disease.
Environmental: herbal nephrotoxins, schistosomiasis, occupational exposures.

sections.p: Patients often present with vague constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, fatigue) plus organ‑specific complaints. In low‑resource settings, delayed presentation is common.
b: Ask about travel, animal contact, water source, and traditional medicines.
Examine for pallor, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, edema, and organomegaly.

sections.p: Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; when unavailable, use bedside alternatives.

t.b: Is there anaemia, leukocytosis or thrombocytopenia? Guides infection vs marrow suppression.
Is malaria present? Positive test confirms Plasmodium infection; negative with high suspicion → microscopy or treat empirically.
Is there pneumonia, pleural effusion, or TB cavitation? Guides antibiotics and isolation.
Is renal function impaired? Determines drug dosing and need for dialysis.
Is there protein, blood or glucose? Helps detect nephropathy, infection, or diabetes.
Is the patient HIV positive? Positive result alters infection work‑up and prophylaxis.

sections.p: Identify signs that indicate imminent deterioration and require urgent escalation.
b: Altered mental status, hypotension, tachypnoea, oliguria.
Severe anaemia (Hb <70 g/L), uncontrolled sepsis, massive haemoptysis.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care and monitor for complications. Choose drugs that are affordable, have a wide safety margin, and are available in oral or injectable form.
b: Antibiotics: use amoxicillin‑clavulanate or ceftriaxone for community‑acquired infections; avoid fluoroquinolones in patients with cardiac arrhythmia risk.
Antimalarials: artemisinin‑based combination therapy; avoid quinine in patients with G6PD deficiency.
Antiretrovirals: start first‑line tenofovir‑lamivudine‑efavirenz; avoid zidovudine in severe anaemia.
Fluid resuscitation: isotonic saline 20 mL/kg bolus; stop if pulmonary oedema develops.
Blood transfusion: give packed red cells for Hb <70 g/L with symptoms.

sections.p: Arrange scheduled reviews, reinforce preventive measures, and educate on early warning signs.
b: Vaccinate against hepatitis B, pneumococcus, and influenza.
Promote insecticide‑treated nets and intermittent preventive treatment for malaria.
Screen for hypertension and diabetes annually.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic common presentations in low‑resource settings.
b: Tuberculosis vs. lung cancer – TB often has night sweats, weight loss, and cavitation; cancer less likely in young patients.
Malaria vs. viral fever – malaria shows periodic chills and positive rapid test; viral illnesses lack parasitaemia.

sections.p: Laboratory or bedside findings that may be falsely normal or abnormal.
b: Malaria rapid test can be negative early; consider microscopy if suspicion high.
Serum creatinine may be normal in early acute kidney injury; monitor urine output.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe chest pain radiating to arm or jaw

faq.q: Why is a focused history more important than a long list of symptoms?
faq.a: It narrows the differential quickly, saves time, and highlights epidemiologic risk factors common in low‑resource settings.

faq.q: What if the chest X‑ray machine is broken?
faq.a: Use bedside lung auscultation, percussion, and observe for pleural effusion signs; treat empirically if clinical picture fits.

faq.q: When should I start antiretroviral therapy in a newly diagnosed HIV patient?
faq.a: Immediately after diagnosis, unless there is an acute opportunistic infection requiring stabilization first.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with fever, chills, and cough; sputum smear unavailable – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Use malaria rapid test and chest X‑ray if possible; treat presumptively for malaria if high prevalence and negative smear.

A patient with known sickle‑cell disease develops sudden chest pain and dyspnoea; what red‑flag must you look for and how will you manage it? — Look for acute chest syndrome (new infiltrate, hypoxia); start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, oxygen, and consider blood transfusion.

You receive a lab report showing normal creatinine but the patient is oliguric; what does this indicate and what is your immediate action? — Early AKI can have normal creatinine; monitor urine output, give fluid bolus, and arrange repeat labs.

A pregnant woman in her second trimester presents with fever and jaundice; which infections are most likely and what test would you order first? — Consider malaria, hepatitis B, and leptospirosis; perform malaria rapid test and hepatitis B surface antigen.

During a ward round you find a patient on ceftriaxone who develops a rash and eosinophilia; what is the likely diagnosis and next step? — Likely drug‑induced hypersensitivity; stop ceftriaxone and switch to a non‑beta‑lactam antibiotic.

A 60‑year‑old hypertensive man with chronic cough has a chest X‑ray showing upper‑lobe cavitation; what is the most probable diagnosis and why? — Tuberculosis, because cavitation in the upper lobes is classic in endemic areas and fits constitutional symptoms.

You need to start anticoagulation for a patient with atrial fibrillation but the INR is unavailable; how do you decide on therapy? — Use clinical CHA₂DS₂‑VASc score; if high risk, start low‑dose aspirin as a bridge while arranging INR.

A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with fever and back pain; what serious complication must you exclude and how? — Vertebral osteomyelitis; obtain blood cultures and MRI if available, otherwise start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A systematic history and focused physical exam uncover the pattern of organ involvement, epidemiologic clues and red‑flag features that guide further testing in low‑resource settings.
b: Onset, duration and pattern of fever (continuous, intermittent, night sweats).
Cough: productive vs dry, haemoptysis, diurnal variation, exposure to smoke or biomass.
Weight loss, appetite change, night sweats – suggest chronic infection or malignancy.
Chest pain: pleuritic, retro‑sternal, radiating to back – assess for pleural, cardiac or musculoskeletal cause.
Dyspnoea: orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, exertional limits – evaluate cardiac vs pulmonary origin.
Travel, occupation, animal contact, water source, traditional medicines – identify tropical or environmental exposures.
HIV status, known TB, diabetes, sickle‑cell disease, pregnancy – modify differential and investigations.

t.b: Look for pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, edema; positive findings suggest anaemia, hepatic disease, chronic hypoxia or systemic infection; cannot quantify severity without labs.

t.a: Respiratory examination – inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation
t.b: Identify breath‑sound abnormalities (crackles, wheeze, pleural rub), percussion dullness (effusion) or hyperresonance (pneumothorax); a positive pleural rub suggests pleuritis, but cannot differentiate cause without imaging.

t.a: Cardiac exam – apex beat, murmurs, JVP, peripheral pulses
t.b: Elevated JVP, displaced apex, S3 gallop point to heart failure; a murmur may indicate valvular disease; bedside exam cannot grade severity of valve stenosis without echocardiography.

t.a: Abdominal exam – inspection, palpation, percussion, shifting dullness
t.b: Shifting dullness confirms free fluid; fluid thrill suggests large ascites; cannot determine albumin gradient or cause without paracentesis.
Pitting oedema in lower limbs indicates volume overload or hypoalbuminaemia; cannot differentiate cardiac from renal cause without further tests.
Altered mental status or focal signs are red flags for sepsis, meningitis or stroke; bedside cannot localise lesion without imaging.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select investigations that answer a single clinical question; interpret results with locally validated cut‑offs and know alternatives when a test is unavailable.
b: Full blood count – anaemia (Hb <70 g/L), leukocytosis (>12 ×10⁹/L) or lymphopenia; malaria smear or rapid test if fever and endemic.
Serum creatinine and electrolytes – assess renal function; oliguria with normal creatinine suggests pre‑renal AKI.
Liver function tests – AST/ALT >2 × ULN, bilirubin >50 µmol/L, albumin <30 g/L; pattern helps differentiate hepatitis, cholestasis or sepsis‑related injury.
Chest X‑ray – infiltrates, cavitation, pleural effusion; upper‑lobe cavitation suggests TB, but consider fungal disease.
Sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF (if available) – detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance; if unavailable, use clinical scoring and chest X‑ray.
Urine dipstick – protein, blood, leukocyte esterase; positive protein with oedema may indicate nephrotic syndrome.
Serum albumin and ascitic fluid analysis – calculate SAAG (serum‑ascites albumin gradient). SAAG ≥11 g/L indicates portal hypertension; <11 g/L suggests peritoneal infection or malignancy.

t.b: Answers whether Plasmodium falciparum is present; positive test confirms infection; if unavailable, treat empirically based on epidemiology and fever pattern.
Determines HIV status; positive result triggers universal ART initiation; if unavailable, use clinical staging and refer for confirmatory testing.
Screen for tissue hypoperfusion; lactate >2 mmol/L suggests severe sepsis; if unavailable, rely on clinical shock signs.
Identifies bloodstream pathogens; growth guides definitive antibiotics; if unavailable, start broad‑spectrum empiric therapy based on local antibiogram.
Assesses oxygenation and acid‑base status; PaO₂ <60 mmHg indicates hypoxaemia; if unavailable, use SpO₂ and clinical work of breathing.
Evaluates cardiac function, pericardial effusion, valvular lesions; if unavailable, use clinical signs of heart failure and chest X‑ray.

sections.p: Combine clinical pattern, epidemiology and investigations to reach a working diagnosis, then apply validated severity scores for triage and management.
b: Diagnose community‑acquired pneumonia when cough, fever, infiltrate on chest X‑ray and no recent hospitalization; severity by CURB‑65 (confusion, urea >7 mmol/L, respiratory rate ≥30, BP <90/60, age ≥65).
Diagnose decompensated cirrhosis with ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy; stage by Child‑Pugh (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy).
Stage HIV infection by WHO clinical stage (I–IV) when CD4 count unavailable; treat all stages with ART.

t.b: Answers inpatient vs outpatient need; score 0–1 low risk (outpatient), 2 moderate (short admission), ≥3 high risk (consider ICU).
Answers prognosis of chronic liver disease; Class A (5‑6 points) good, B (7‑9) intermediate, C (10‑15) poor; guides transplant referral.
Answers whether ascites is due to portal hypertension; SAAG ≥11 g/L = portal hypertension, <11 g/L = peritoneal disease.
Answers need for parenteral therapy and intensive monitoring; presence of any criterion mandates IV artesunate.

sections.p: Several diseases mimic the presenting syndrome; use key discriminators to avoid misdiagnosis, especially when investigations are limited.
b: Pulmonary TB vs bacterial pneumonia – TB: chronic cough >2 weeks, weight loss, night sweats, upper‑lobe cavitation; pneumonia: acute fever, productive sputum, lobar consolidation.
Heart failure vs severe pneumonia – HF: elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, S3 gallop; pneumonia: localized crackles, fever, leukocytosis.
Malaria vs viral febrile illness – malaria: periodic chills, positive rapid test, thrombocytopenia; viral: rash, lymphocytosis, negative malaria test.
Ascites from cirrhosis vs tuberculous peritonitis – cirrhosis: SAAG ≥11 g/L, low albumin, stigmata of chronic liver disease; TB: SAAG <11 g/L, lymphocyte‑rich fluid, high ADA.

t.b: Key points: chronicity, night sweats, weight loss, upper‑lobe cavitation, GeneXpert positivity for TB; bacterial pneumonia shows acute onset, higher neutrophil count, lobar infiltrate.
Key points: raised JVP, peripheral oedema, S3, cardiomegaly on X‑ray for HF; fever, leukocytosis, localized crackles for pneumonia.
Key points: positive malaria rapid test, periodic chills, thrombocytopenia for malaria; rash, lymphocytosis, negative malaria test for viral infection.
Key points: SAAG ≥11 g/L, low serum albumin for cirrhosis; SAAG <11 g/L, lymphocyte‑predominant fluid, high ADA for TB peritonitis.

sections.p: Begin with immediate stabilization, then target the underlying cause, monitor response, and decide on escalation or referral.
b: 1. Airway, breathing, circulation: oxygen if SpO2 <94%, IV access, isotonic fluid bolus 20 mL/kg if hypovolemic
2. Definitive therapy:
- Infection – start empiric antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + amoxicillin‑clavulanate) then narrow per culture
- Malaria – artemisinin‑based combination (artemether‑lumefantrine) even in pregnancy
- Sepsis – early goal‑directed therapy, source control
- Anemia – transfuse packed cells if Hb <70 g/L with symptoms
- Organ failure – renal replacement if oliguria persists, ventilatory support if respiratory distress

t.b: Fluoroquinolones in children and pregnancy; quinine in G6PD without monitoring; nephrotoxic drugs in renal impairment
Hemodynamics, urine output, mental status, lactate, organ function scores (e.g., SOFA)

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognise key adverse effects and interactions, and act promptly.
b: 1. Antibiotics – watch for rash, eosinophilia, neutropenia; stop and switch if severe
2. Antimalarials – monitor for hemolysis in G6PD, liver enzymes; repeat CBC
3. Antiretrovirals – avoid zidovudine in severe anemia; monitor for lipodystrophy
4. NSAIDs – avoid in renal failure, monitor creatinine
5. Diuretics – watch for electrolyte imbalance, hypotension

t.b: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ritonavir) raise levels of protease inhibitors; adjust dosing
If rash + eosinophilia, stop ceftriaxone, start antihistamine, consider alternative

sections.p: Identify red‑flag complications early and refer when thresholds are crossed.
b: 1. Shock – persistent MAP <65 mmHg despite fluids, need vasopressors
2. Acute kidney injury – oliguria <400 mL/24h, creatinine rise >50%
3. Severe anemia – Hb <70 g/L with tachycardia or chest pain
5. CNS involvement – altered mental status, seizures, focal deficits

t.b: Transfer to higher level of care if any complication persists after 6–8 h of treatment
For surgical source control, advanced dialysis, or specialist consultation

sections.p: Adjust assessment and management for comorbidities and contextual factors.
b: 1. HIV – broaden differential to opportunistic infections, use ART regardless of CD4
2. TB – consider co‑infection, use rifampicin‑based regimens with caution for drug interactions
3. Malnutrition – lower drug clearance, higher infection risk, consider micronutrient support
4. Pregnancy – use ACTs, avoid teratogenic drugs, monitor fetal growth
5. Diabetes – higher risk of sepsis, monitor glucose, adjust insulin
6. Herbal remedies – possible hepatotoxicity, drug interactions, ask about use
7. Alcohol – risk of hepatic injury, adjust dosing of hepatically metabolised drugs
8. Renal/liver failure – dose adjust, avoid nephrotoxic or hepatotoxic agents
9. Age extremes – altered pharmacokinetics, higher frailty in elderly, developmental differences in children

sections.p: Tailor investigations and therapy to children, pregnancy, elderly, HIV, and low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Children – use weight‑based dosing, prefer oral antibiotics when possible, monitor growth
2. Pregnancy – avoid teratogenic drugs, use ACTs, monitor fetal heart rate
3. Elderly – reduce polypharmacy, monitor for falls, adjust for comorbidities
4. HIV patients – start ART immediately, monitor for drug‑drug interactions
5. Low‑resource settings – rely on clinical scoring, use WHO case definitions, prioritize essential drugs

sections.p: Sample questions covering bedside, investigations, management, complications, and special factors.
b: 1. A 28‑year‑old pregnant woman presents with fever and jaundice. Which infections should you consider and what first‑line treatment is safe?
2. A patient with known HIV develops a rash and eosinophilia after starting ceftriaxone. What is the likely diagnosis and next step?
3. How would you interpret a serum‑ascites albumin gradient of 12 g/L?
4. A 65‑year‑old man with chronic cough has a chest X‑ray showing upper‑lobe cavitation. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial therapy?
5. A 45‑year‑old woman with severe anemia (Hb 65 g/L) and tachycardia is admitted. What is the threshold for transfusion and what monitoring is required?
6. A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with fever and back pain. What serious complication must be ruled out and how?
7. In a setting without a creatinine assay, how would you assess renal function in a patient with oliguria?
8. A patient on ART develops hepatotoxicity. Which drug class is most likely responsible and what is the management?
9. What bedside signs would you use to differentiate ascites from pleural effusion?
10. A patient with septic shock is not responding to fluids. What is the next step in management?

facts: CURB‑65 score ≥3 indicates high mortality risk in community‑acquired pneumonia
Sepsis defined by qSOFA ≥2 or SIRS + organ dysfunction
Severe anaemia Hb <70 g/L with symptoms requires transfusion
Artemether‑lumefantrine first‑line for uncomplicated falciparum malaria in all trimesters
Quinine can be used in G6PD deficiency with caution and close monitoring for haemolysis
Oliguria <400 mL/day in adults signals acute kidney injury

vivas.q: Define sepsis and explain the qSOFA criteria.
vivas.a: Sepsis is life‑threatening organ dysfunction from infection. qSOFA: systolic BP ≤100 mmHg, respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation (GCS <15). A score of 2 or more predicts poor outcome.

vivas.q: Why is quinine used with caution in G6PD deficiency?
vivas.a: Quinine can trigger haemolysis; monitoring hemoglobin and reticulocytes is essential. The risk is lower than with primaquine but still significant.
Score 2 suggests moderate severity; admit for monitoring, give IV antibiotics, and consider ICU if deterioration.

vivas.q: A patient with known sickle‑cell disease presents with sudden chest pain and dyspnoea. What red flag requires immediate action?
vivas.a: Oxygen saturation <90% or hypotension indicates acute chest syndrome; start oxygen, analgesia, antibiotics, and consider exchange transfusion.

vivas.q: Explain the rationale for starting ART in all HIV patients regardless of CD4 count.
vivas.a: Early treatment reduces viral replication, prevents opportunistic infections, and lowers transmission risk. WHO 2023 guidelines endorse 'treat all'.

vivas.q: A 60‑year‑old hypertensive man has a chest X‑ray with upper‑lobe cavitation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: Pulmonary tuberculosis; start RIPE therapy and investigate for drug resistance.

vivas.q: What bedside sign indicates ascites and how is it elicited?
vivas.a: Shifting dullness: patient supine, tap lower flank; if dullness shifts to upper flank when upright, fluid is present.

vivas.q: Why is a normal creatinine not reassuring in an oliguric patient?
vivas.a: Creatinine may lag; oliguria indicates acute kidney injury. Assess urine output, electrolytes, and consider renal replacement if worsening.

vivas.q: Describe the management steps for a patient with severe anaemia (Hb 65 g/L) and chest pain.
vivas.a: Give packed red cells to raise Hb >70 g/L, monitor vitals, treat underlying cause (e.g., myocardial infarction), and reassess for transfusion needs.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate bacterial sepsis from viral sepsis clinically?
vivas.a: Bacterial sepsis often has higher fever, rigors, and organ dysfunction; viral may have milder fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy. Lab: high neutrophils vs lymphocytes.

vivas.q: A patient on ceftriaxone develops a rash and eosinophilia. What is the likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS); stop ceftriaxone, start steroids if severe.

vivas.q: Explain the significance of a serum‑ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1 g/dL.
vivas.a: High SAAG indicates portal hypertension; low SAAG suggests exudative ascites from infection or malignancy.

vivas.q: What is the management of a patient with acute kidney injury and normal creatinine?
vivas.a: Check urine output, electrolytes, and imaging; consider contrast nephropathy or pre‑renal causes; initiate fluid resuscitation if appropriate.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old man presents with fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Chest X‑ray shows upper‑lobe infiltrate. Which drug is first‑line for treatment?
mcqs.e: Isoniazid is part of the RIPE regimen for TB.

mcqs.q: A patient with G6PD deficiency is prescribed quinine. What monitoring is essential?
A patient with acute chest pain and dyspnoea has oxygen saturation 88% on room air. What is the next step?
Which of the following is a red flag for severe malaria?

cases.v: A 52‑year‑old man with chronic cough presents with fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Chest X‑ray shows upper‑lobe cavitation. He is HIV negative.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

qs.a: Sputum AFB smear and culture; GeneXpert for rapid detection.

qs.q: What is a key red flag that would require ICU admission?
qs.a: Respiratory rate >30/min, hypotension, or altered mental status indicating sepsis.

mistakes: Assuming normal creatinine rules out AKI in oliguria
Using quinine without monitoring haemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Starting ART only when CD4 <200 or viral load >1000 copies/mL
Treating uncomplicated malaria with chloroquine in areas of resistance
Ignoring CURB‑65 score and discharging severe pneumonia
Misinterpreting SAAG >1.1 as always cirrhosis without considering portal hypertension causes
Overlooking altered mental status as a red flag in sepsis
Failing to give oxygen to hypoxic patients with chest pain

Why is quinine used with caution in G6PD deficiency? — Quinine can trigger haemolysis; monitoring hemoglobin and reticulocytes is essential. The risk is lower than with primaquine but still significant.
Interpret a CURB‑65 score of 2. — Score 2 suggests moderate severity; admit for monitoring, give IV antibiotics, and consider ICU if deterioration.
